newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin may walk as communists march in Moscow.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin may walk as communists march in Moscow.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin could be back on his feet on Thursday, just two days after open heart surgery which he hopes will give him a new lease on life to guide Russia further from its communist past.
Doctors are pleased with the 65-year-old leader's progress and said they may give in to his requests for a move to a more comfortable clinic on Thursday and let him try a little walking.
His communist opponents will march through Moscow to mark the 79th anniversary of the 1917 Bolshevik revolution.

But the turnout is more likely to highlight how far support for communism has been undermined in the five years since the end of the Soviet Union than provide evidence that Russians are ready take to the streets in protest at bewildering hardships.
"He is doing very well," one of the American doctors who have been in Moscow to monitor Yeltsin's treatment said.
"Everything is going very well, without any complications," Professor George Noon of Baylor College of Medicine told Reuters late on Wednesday. He could start walking on Thursday, he added.

If an examination due on Thursday morning confirmed the president was continuing to make progress, Noon said he could be granted his request to move from the intensive care unit at the Cardiology Research Centre, where doctors operated on him on Tuesday.
It is a tribute to medical science but also to the robust constitition of a man with a reputation for sheer hard work.

Yeltsin felt well enough to take back his full presidential powers from Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin less than 24 hours after handing them over. He has been pestering staff to let him move to the elite Central Clinical Hospital nearby.
The president spent time in a suite there before the operation and was treated for heart trouble there last year.
Reporters outside the Cardiology Research Centre at midnight (2100 GMT) on Wednesday said all was quiet. Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky will brief the media at midday (0900 GMT).
Yeltsin's wife Naina, visibly relieved, told Russian television on Wednesday evening she was able to smile again.
The president was no longer attached to artificial tubes, which should allow him to get out of bed and walk. His wife's problem now was stopping him exerting himself too soon.

Pioneering U.S. heart surgeon Michael DeBakey, 88, who advised on the seven-hour operation to graft in veins that bypass five blockages in Yeltsin's cardiac arteries, said he could even be back on the tennis court in four months.
But he urged him to be patient and follow doctors' orders.
Even Yeltsin's political foes wished him well on the eve of celebrations of the overthrow of the tsarist regime.
Communist Gennady Zyuganov, beaten in a run-off for the presidency in July, said: "He must now care more about health."
But at a rally and concert for 3-4,000 mostly elderly party faithful on Wednesday evening, Zyuganov returned to the attack.
"The country is run by thieves and drunkards," he said, standing beneath a giant poster of Lenin and recalling the glory days of the Soviet superpower.

Yet on the evidence of recent years, few of the 40 million who voted for Zyuganov in June are likely to take advantage of Thursday's public holiday to march in protest at the deep economic crisis which has left many workers unpaid for months.

A wave of strikes and protests called by trade unions on Tuesday was poorly supported. Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov insisted on Wednesday there was little chance of mutiny in the armed forces despite the troops having had no wages for weeks.
The communists will respect a ban on gathering in Red Square, scene of huge Revolution Day parades in Soviet times.

Just as Western leaders have wished Yeltsin a speedy recovery in the hope he can restore order to the economy and end the anxiety caused by Kremlin in-fighting in his absence, the Russian leader welcomed the continuity in Washington assured by President Bill Clinton's reelection to the White House.
"In the name of the Russian leadership and for myself personally, I congratulate you on your election," Yeltsin, who likes to call Clinton "my friend Bill", said in a statement.
Doctors say Yeltsin could be back at his desk in a couple of months but caution that his health will need careful monitoring in the next few days in case complications should arise.
